results.releaseNotes: Small & important bug fixes for an ongoing research project inside one sec.
results.description:
Willpower is not enough against social media algorithms!

That’s why I made one sec:

one sec adds friction to distracting apps to make them less appealing…long-term!

This principle works really well: we have gained scientific evidence in numerous research studies with the Max-Planck Institute, with the German and Danish government, and in dozens more scientific collaborations:

one sec has incredible effects on your screen time: app usage drops by 57% on average!

…just read our App Store reviews or try it for yourself if you don’t believe me (…you should really try it)!


How is one sec different from Screen Time limits or app blockers?
- one sec DELAYS access to distracting apps instead of blocking apps completely – that’s an important difference psychologically.
- This way, we solve the screen time problem at its roots: long-term & sustainably!
- one sec is always on, and makes using social media just slightly more annoying…so you’ll end up using it only when you actually have a reason!


Which apps can I use with one sec?
- You can set up one sec with any app you’d like to use less / more intentional.
- Most popular use-cases are: social media, games, video streaming, dating, stock/coin trading, adult content.
- Using one sec with one app of your choice if completely free, for more you’ll need to purchase one sec pro (we also need to finance development of our app!).


What if I get stuck scrolling?
- No worries, one sec offers a Doom Scroll Emergency Brake: We call it Re-Intervention.
- After a set time (e.g. 5 minutes) you’ll be kicked out of social media, and you’ll have to go through an intervention again to unlock more time.


Where can I learn more about the scientific background of one sec?
→ https://one-sec.app/research


Can I use one sec to interrupt access to websites as well?
→ Yes, one sec offers a free Safari extension as well.


How does one sec work technically?
- one sec uses Shortcuts Automation to toggle a deep breath animation whenever you open one of the configured apps (Instagram, Twitter, YouTube…).
- This breaks unconscious social media habits short-term (literally, as soon as you have set it up) and even helps long-term by adding more friction when opening these apps.


Integrations:
- Structured: one sec blocks apps during unfinished tasks.
- LENGO: learn vocabulary to unlock social media.


I developed one sec for myself in 2020…and it worked so well I decided to upload it to the App Store.

Especially for people with ADHD one sec is a great tool to gain back control for incredible focus and concentration.

– Frederik

Start a hard stop and your apps are shut until the time is up. Not paused. Not
until you change your mind. Until it is up.

Most blockers can be undone in two taps: edit the schedule, or delete it.
Hardstop cannot. While a block runs, the rules that define it are frozen the
schedule cannot be edited to end early, disabled or deleted, and blocked apps
cannot be removed from the list.

Pay once. No subscription, no account, no data collected. Everything runs on
your iPhone.

Block now, or set hours that repeat

Tap once and pick a length: fifteen minutes, an hour, three hours. The apps you
chose are shut for that long, with no schedule to build first. Make it a hard
stop and there is no way out at all no wait, no pass, no cancel button.

Schedules do the hours you already know about: a start time, an end time, and
the days it repeats. Blocking continues whether or not Hardstop is running, and
survives restarting your iPhone.

Three ways in, and each one costs more

Outside a hard stop you can ask to be let into a blocked app. Asking starts a
wait rather than opening it, and when the wait is over you have to come back and
ask again. That second, deliberate step is the point.

Every pass after the first in the same block costs more: thirty seconds becomes
ninety, then three minutes. And you only get three per block. The first slip of
an afternoon stays cheap. The fourth is not offered.

A pass is temporary too. After sixteen minutes the block returns on its own,
without you having to remember to put it back.

A record of what actually happened

When a block ends, Hardstop writes down whether you saw it through or asked your
way in, and how many times. Not screen time statistics a record of you against
your own rules. It never leaves your iPhone.

Strict mode

With strict mode on, every block behaves like a hard stop, and strict mode
cannot be switched off while one is running.

Deleting Hardstop would still lift a block. No app on iOS can prevent that, and
this one will not claim otherwise.

What it uses

Hardstop blocks apps through Apple's Screen Time framework, which runs entirely
on your device. It asks for access for you, as an adult managing your own
iPhone. It is not a parental-controls app: it cannot see, manage or report on
another person's device.

Free and unlocked

Blocking is never the thing you pay for. The free version blocks as many apps
and categories as you like, on one schedule, with hard stops and the record
included. The unlock is a single purchase adding unlimited schedules, strict
mode, and a wait length of your choosing. It is not a subscription. Nothing
renews.

Privacy

Hardstop has no account, no server and no analytics. Your schedules and the apps
you block never leave your iPhone, because there is nowhere for them to go.

Perimeter is the first comprehensive location-based screen time app. Set a rule once and forget about it: Perimeter turns distracting apps off where you want to be present and focused, and leaves them on when you're on the go and need your phone to work in our fast-paced world.

A NOTE FROM THE FOUNDER
I'm Jack, founder of Perimeter, and I have been dreaming of building this app for over 10 years. I'm passionate about finding and developing solutions to help people regain balance with their devices. Perimeter is made by a small team that shares that mission.

THE PROBLEM: CONSTANT CONNECTION
We used to have TVs with a few channels that were on for an hour or two per day, and they stayed in the living room. We had a landline phone at home connected to the wall and a desktop computer in our office. Now we have all three combined into one device, with an infinite catalog of entertainment, news, and communication that follows us everywhere: into our kitchens, our bedrooms, our offices, and our friends' and family's homes.

Our brains naturally respond to the environments we are in, good or bad. We think differently at the office vs. at home vs. out on the street. Until now, our smartphone has been configured the exact same way in all of those places.

A DIFFERENT PHONE FOR EVERY PLACE
Perimeter blocks distractions inside or outside the places where you want to be focused or present. It turns your phone into a different device at home vs. the office vs. in public, returning each place to what it's meant to be: home for rest and family time, the office for work.
- Draw a perimeter around a place: home, the office, the bedroom
- Choose the apps that don't belong there
- Walk in and they pause. Walk out and they're back
No more scrolling Instagram at work or at home. No more checking work email at home.

SET IT ONCE. IT JUST WORKS.
Unlike other screen time apps or Apple's built-in Screen Time, Perimeter doesn't block apps all the time or on a set schedule. Those lead to problems: needing apps when traveling or at work, rules that are easy to bypass, and the same blocking everywhere you go.

Perimeter is context-aware. No more setting limits and then not being able to check in for a flight, authenticate a login, or find a taxi. Your full phone works on the go, and keeps things in check where it matters most.

MORE THAN WILLPOWER
For people who want more than willpower to regain control of their screen time, Perimeter has strong locking mechanisms:
- A settings passcode, or hand your phone to someone you trust and let them set one you don't know
- Turning Perimeter on never needs the passcode. Turning it off always does
- Fail-safe by design: if location is switched off or permission is changed, apps stay blocked
- Optional short breaks that can't be extended by quitting the app or changing the clock

ONE STEP ON THE JOURNEY TO FREEDOM
Perimeter is a first step. The goal is to keep taking steps toward more freedom from screens, going far beyond Perimeter: leaving your phone outside of your bedroom, setting Downtime for better sleep, having an accountability partner, rediscovering other hobbies, and starting to prefer time off the device to time on it.

Pair it with a less distracting screen (a black and white filter) and a Downtime that reduces your phone to the basics while you sleep. Combine it with iOS Screen Time limits for the most comprehensive system, with Perimeter providing the context for what should be blocked when.

PRIVATE BY DESIGN
No account. No servers. No analytics. Your location never leaves your iPhone. Apple's Screen Time pauses the apps, and Perimeter never sees what you do inside them.

FREE FOR A LIMITED TIME
We're providing Perimeter free of charge for a limited time, in the hope of introducing the world to a new paradigm of context-aware screen time: like having different devices tuned for the different places you go.

results.description:
Every app blocker has an off switch. At 11 p.m. you will find it. ScrollCop is a friendly cop for your phone: you decide, before the urge, who gets to let your apps out.

BLOCK APPS IN TWO TAPS
Tap the apps that eat your time: Instagram, TikTok, YouTube, Reddit, X, or any app on your phone, plus whole categories and websites. Pick how long. The apps disappear from your Home Screen and won't open until time's up. It runs on Apple's Screen Time, so it holds even if you close ScrollCop. Try to open one and you get pulled over.

YOU CHOOSE WHO CAN END IT EARLY
Every block starts as "Nobody", so it really holds. Change it with one tap:
• Me: end it whenever you want.
• Nobody: not even you. It opens when time's up.
• A friend: ScrollCop texts them a one-time PIN. Only that PIN ends the block early. Your friend doesn't need the app.

Want it even stronger? Give a friend your key, and codes come only from their phone. Locks hold even if you change the date or time, and ScrollCop can't be deleted while a locked block runs. Schedules start locked too.

SCHEDULES THAT RUN EVERY DAY
Block apps at the same time every day, automatically, even with ScrollCop closed. Give each schedule its own apps: games during study time, social apps at dinner, everything at bedtime. Start from Bedtime, Mornings, Work hours, Study time or Dinner, or make your own.

A COP THAT CHEERS YOU ON
Over 5,000 short, original lines turn up around the app: on Home, while a block runs, on the screen you see when you try to open a blocked app, and when a block is done. Some are jokes, some are pep talks, all of them are on your side.

165 THINGS TO DO INSTEAD
Bored? Stressed? Up too late? ScrollCop suggests three small things that fit the time you have and the time of day: stretch for three minutes, write a two-line poem, tidy one drawer, lay out tomorrow's clothes. Tap "Show me three others" for more.

SOS FOR THE MOMENT IT HITS
Tap "I feel the urge" and ScrollCop asks what you actually need: bored, stressed, tired, lonely, avoiding something. It gives you one small thing to do instead, then checks whether the pull dropped.

BOREDOM GYM
Scrolling trained you to fill every gap. This trains the opposite: short exercises in sitting with nothing, thirty seconds first, then longer.

YOUR WEEK AT A GLANCE
One sentence about your week, a simple chart and three plain numbers, like "45 min blocked today" and "12 days in a row without your blocked apps". Everything else is one tap away, each number with a line saying what it means. Counted on your phone. A slip is data, not failure. No guilt notifications.

PRIVATE BY DESIGN
No account. No server. No ads, no analytics, no subscription. Apple's Screen Time gives ScrollCop opaque tokens, so it can't see which apps you use. Export or delete everything whenever you like.

Free. Made in Canada. A behaviour-change tool, not medical advice.

Enough for Now is an app blocker for people who want fewer distractions without turning their phone into another complicated project. Choose the apps or categories that tend to pull you away, decide when the lock should run, and let Apple Screen Time add useful friction during that window.

Use it for a focused work session, an evening study block, a meeting, writing time, or the part of the night when one quick check usually becomes another hour of scrolling. Every lock is created by you, with a clear start, a clear end, and a visible reason for being there.

START A QUICK LOCK

When you need to begin now, Quick Lock keeps the setup short. Choose apps or categories, pick a duration, add an optional note to yourself, and start. The Home screen shows the active rule and its end time, while the Screen Time shield reminds you why the selected app is unavailable.

BUILD RULES AROUND REAL LIFE

Enough for Now supports three schedule types:

- Countdown for a one-time focus window
- Recurring for routines such as weekdays, study hours, or bedtime
- Date Range for a specific start and end date

Recurring rules can cross midnight, so a bedtime rule can begin at night and finish the next morning. Countdown rules also support a custom hour-and-minute duration. The current version supports up to three rules, keeping the list useful without turning setup into a planning system of its own.

SEE WHAT IS ACTIVE

The Home screen shows the current lock state, active rules, saved notes, and when the longest-running rule will end. Rule details show the schedule, selected scope, local status events, and any edit-protection period. If Screen Time permission or schedule registration needs attention, the app explains what happened and offers a way to reapply the rules.

MAKE IMPORTANT RULES HARDER TO CHANGE

For recurring routines that matter, you can enable rule edit protection for 1, 7, or 30 days. While that protection is active, the rule remains available to review but cannot be edited, paused, or deleted from the normal controls. Confirmation uses Face ID, Touch ID, or the device passcode when available, and the end time is shown before you enable it.

OPTIONAL UNINSTALL PROTECTION

Enough for Now can also request Apple's Screen Time uninstall-protection setting for 1, 7, or 30 days. This is a user-enabled, time-limited layer of friction. The app shows whether iOS reports the setting as active and when it expires. It does not override iOS, Screen Time authorization, or device-owner controls.

PRIVATE BY DEFAULT

Your rules, schedules, selected Screen Time tokens, and local status history stay on your iPhone. Enough for Now does not require an account, developer server, cloud sync, advertising SDK, or third-party analytics. There is no social feed and no data-selling business model.

Enough for Now uses Apple's Screen Time frameworks. App selections stay behind Apple's protected system interface, and the app does not read content inside selected apps.

FREE CORE FEATURES, NO SUBSCRIPTION

The current version is free and does not include a subscription or paid feature gate. An optional Tip Jar lets you support continued development with a one-time consumable purchase. Tips do not unlock features, raise limits, or change how app blocking works.

LANGUAGES

Use Enough for Now in English, Simplified Chinese, or Traditional Chinese.

REQUIREMENTS AND BOUNDARIES

Enough for Now requires iOS 17 or later and Screen Time authorization to block selected apps or categories. Blocking depends on Apple Screen Time services and the permission you grant. If authorization is removed, the app cannot continue applying those restrictions.

Enough for Now is built for self-directed focus. It does not monitor another person's messages, browsing, location, or private content, and it does not make medical or productivity guarantees. It gives you a clear way to decide, in advance, when distracting apps should be harder to open.

results.description:
Verboten blocks the apps you choose. You pick them once, and they stop opening.

Not a timer you can dismiss. Not a nag screen. iOS itself holds the door,
through the same Screen Time machinery Apple uses for parental controls, 
so a blocked app meets a shield instead of a feed, and there is nothing to swipe past.

    WHAT IT DOES

Pick your apps. Instagram, TikTok, YouTube, whatever your evenings
disappear into. One switch holds all of them.

Block only when it matters. Add a window — evenings, work hours, overnight
— and blocking applies then and not otherwise. A window can cover every app
or a single one. With no window, it is simply always on.

Two minutes, not the evening. Need an app right now? Take a couple of
minutes. It shuts again by itself, and the setting returns to Never — so a
moment of weakness never quietly becomes a permanent exception.

Pause on your terms. Everything opens for as long as you chose, then
blocking comes back on its own. No decision to remember.

Something better to read. An optional bulletin of the day's AI news from
real newsrooms — grouped so one story isn't repeated five times, and ten
stories long. It ends, which is the whole point. Turn it off and the app fetches nothing at all.

A line worth reading. Every block shows one: a fact, a thought, a reason to look away.

    WHAT IT DOESN'T DO

No account. No sign-in. No analytics, no ads, no trackers.

Nothing about you leaves your phone. Your blocked list, your schedules and
your settings live on the device. On iOS the app cannot even read which
apps you picked; Apple hands it opaque tokens, and that is all it ever sees.

No guilt. Missing your own rules is not a failure state. There is no streak
to break and no score to lose.

Verboten is made by the ReadLoft team.

results.releaseNotes:
Hi folks,

This update comes with some useful new features, design improvements, and under-the-hood improvements.

Focus Spaces & Blocking
- Every Focus Space card now has an on/off switch. Turning a space on first shows what it will block; turning it off asks you to type the stop-early text.
- Focus Spaces now run manually, daily or weekly. A manual space runs until you turn it off, and schedules repeat until you stop them or until a date you choose. This replaces the Timer.
- Turning off a scheduled Focus Space now keeps its schedule, ready to switch back on, instead of deleting it.
- Pause has been replaced by "Turn back on after": each Focus Space can switch itself back on 5 minutes to 24 hours after you stop it, or stay off. The default pause length in Settings has gone with it.
- Quick Start has been removed. Blocking now always starts from a saved Focus Space, and a Quick Start block that is running when you update carries on as a normal Focus Space.
- To stop early, you now type words on every platform, with an estimate of how long it takes. Random gibberish and Max difficulty have been removed.
- A Focus Space that is switched off can now be edited in full, including its Editing option (previously called Strictness).
- Adding a website with "www." now also blocks it without, so www.youtube.com blocks youtube.com too. This also applies to websites in imported Focus Spaces.
- New installs now start with no Focus Spaces, so you set up your own.
- Turning off one Focus Space no longer lifts the blocks of other Focus Spaces that are still running.
- Allow-only Focus Spaces now check Apple's limit of 50 allowed websites and 50 allowed apps across all running spaces together, including when you turn one back on.
- Blocking keeps working when Screen Time's app choices expire. If an app choice cannot be recovered, you are asked to pick it again.
- If Screen Time permission is removed, the app now notices and asks for it again.

Privacy
- Digital Habits: Blocker now sends one anonymous count a day, only on days you use it, so we know how many people use it. It contains nothing about your Focus Spaces, and you can turn it off in Settings under "Send anonymous usage count". The welcome screen explains this under "Private by design".

Fixes & Polish
- The Focus Space cards have been redesigned. Each card shows its status and times, such as "Blocking now" or "Paused until 16:00 tomorrow", and the "Show what it blocks on the card" option now works as described. Duplicate and Delete are at the top of the edit screen (and on right-click on desktop), and undoing a delete brings back the schedule too.
- The design of the create / edit Focus Space screen has been improved. It is now one screen with sections for what to block, when to block and how to stop early.
- Dialogs now dim the screen behind them more clearly, especially in dark mode, and no longer close when a drag ends outside them.
- The design of the iPhone and iPad screens has been improved. Swiping from the left edge goes back, text is no longer selected by accident, Save stays pinned at the bottom of the edit screen, and the stop-early progress bar starts empty.
- Chinese translations have been improved.

Remember that the app is open source — keep your feedback and suggestions coming at https://github.com/digitalhabits/dh-blocker

Cheers,
Ulrik & all of us at Centre for Digital Habits

Focus Firewall puts a shield in front of the apps that eat your day.

Choose what to block. Choose when. That is the whole app.

WHAT IT DOES

• Block Now — one stretch of focus, from 15 minutes to four hours.
• Rules — recurring schedules that run on their own, without you opening anything. "No social media, weekdays 9 to 12."
• A real shield — open a blocked app and you get a full screen and a short written prompt instead.
• Per-app breaks — need one app for a minute? Take a break that opens only that app. Everything else stays shielded.
• Insights — streaks and sessions, counted from what actually happened.

PRIVACY IS THE POINT

No account. No server. No analytics. No third-party SDKs. There is no networking code in this app at all, so there is nothing to send and nowhere to send it.

When you choose apps to block, iOS hands the app opaque tokens — never names. Focus Firewall never learns which apps you picked. Your iPhone draws the icons and names itself.

Your Screen Time data stays inside Apple's own sandbox and never reaches us.

WHAT IT WILL NOT CLAIM

Focus Firewall is not unbreakable, and will not pretend to be. You can always turn off Screen Time access in iOS Settings, and no app can prevent that. Strict Mode makes a rule harder to change while it is running — friction, not a lock.

It also will not tell you how many hours you saved. That would mean knowing what you would otherwise have done. Everything in Insights comes from sessions the app itself recorded.

And when something goes wrong — permission revoked, a shield that did not fire — it says so, instead of showing a reassuring checkmark. Settings › Protection check runs the whole thing end to end and reports each layer.

FREE

One recurring rule, three apps, Block Now up to an hour, real breaks, today's history. Not a trial. It works.

FOCUS FIREWALL PRO

Unlimited rules, website blocking, Strict Mode, daily app budgets, longer and more frequent breaks, weekly insights, the full coach library, your own prompts and shield message, interactive widgets, Face ID lock, and an encrypted backup.

On iPhones with Apple Intelligence, Pro can also write your week up in plain words and turn a sentence into a rule — running entirely on device.

Choose your distractions. Pick everything but your music apps - Spotify or Apple Music - and Blocktape keeps them off for the length of your session.

Press play. One tap starts a session, styled like dropping a cassette into an old tape deck. Your chosen apps disappear.

Track your steps while a session runs, if that's part of your thing.

Blocktape isn't dressed up as a productivity tool. It's built like a time machine - cassette-deck look-and-feel, a UI that feels like the 80s, not like a settings screen. Blocking your phone should feel like a ritual you want to repeat, not a rule you're trying to keep.

Latch puts the apps that pull you in behind a shield for as long as you choose.

You unlock your phone to check one thing. Forty minutes later you are still scrolling. Latch sits in that gap: tap the dial, pick a length, and those apps stop opening until the time runs out.

HOW A LATCH WORKS

Pick the apps and websites you want quiet. Tap the dial. Choose 30 minutes, an hour, two hours, or set your own length. Open something you latched and you get a shield instead, with one button that closes it again.

There is no bypass inside the shield. That is the point. To use the app, you come back to Latch and end the latch on purpose.

GOLDEN LATCH

Some sessions should not be up for negotiation. A Golden Latch starts and holds until time is up. No end-early button. No shield escape. If you need out, you have golden tickets, and you only get three. Every account gets three Golden Latches to try.

SCHEDULES THAT RUN WITHOUT YOU

Deep work at 9. Bedtime at 11. Build a window once and it fires on the weekdays you choose, on time, off time, whether or not Latch is open. Windows can overlap.

SEE WHERE THE DAY WENT

The Focus tab shows your real per-app screen time for any day of the week: total time, pickups, which apps took the hours, and an hour-by-hour split between what distracts you and everything else. WIDGETS, SIRI, SHORTCUTS, AND THE ACTION BUTTON

Start a latch from the Home Screen without opening the app. Watch the countdown on the Lock Screen and in the Dynamic Island. Ask Siri. Map it to the Action Button. Add it as a Shortcut. Widgets for your streak, your weekly goal, your next schedule, and today at a glance.

results.description:
Block Reddit until you've read for 15 minutes. Block Instagram until you've finished a language lesson. Conditioning blocks the apps that waste your time until you've spent a few minutes on the apps that move you towards your long-term goals.

I spent months on iOS Screen Time limits. Every time Twitter got blocked there was a "15 more minutes" button, and I pressed it every single time. It adds a speed bump – Conditioning gives you somewhere else to go.

What finally worked for me was a rule: fifteen minutes of reading before Reddit or Twitter. After a few weeks, "I'm bored" stopped meaning "open Twitter" and started meaning "read a few pages." At my worst I was on Twitter four hours a day. Now I barely open it.

TAKES ABOUT A MINUTE
1. Grant Screen Time permission. One tap and Face ID.
2. Pick the app to block.

YOUR DATA STAYS ON YOUR PHONE
Apple hands Conditioning a random token instead of app names, and every rule and all Screen Time data stays on your device.
